title: Stay Of Conviction Can't Be Sought Only To Contest Elections : Supreme Court
case_name: STATE OF U.P v. MOHAMMAD AZAM KHAN AND ORS
ratio: Courts cannot permit statutory powers to be leveraged to suit political calendars.
summary: The Supreme Court has cautioned that a stay of conviction cannot be sought merely to pursue electoral ambitions or contest upcoming elections, observing that courts cannot permit statutory powers to be leveraged to suit political calendars. At the same time, the Court held that judicial discretion to stay a conviction must be cautiously exercised by balancing the irreversible damage to an individual's personal reputation and dignity against the sanctity of a judicial finding of guilt.

note.Facts: The Supreme Court entertained appeals by Mohammad Abdullah Azam Khan and Dr Tazeen Fatma, seeking a stay of their convictions in a case alleging use of conflicting birth certificates, and a State of U.P. appeal challenging a High Court stay.
note.Issue: Whether a stay of criminal conviction may be granted solely to enable the petitioner to contest elections or pursue electoral ambitions.
note.Held: The Court allowed the stays of conviction pending revision but categorically held that a stay cannot be granted merely on the ground of political or electoral expediency.
note.Principle: A stay of conviction must be exercised with judicial discretion, balancing the irreversible damage to personal dignity (Article 21) against the sanctity of a conviction, and cannot be used as a tool to suit political calendars.
note.Provisions: Section 389(1), Criminal Procedure Code; Article 21 of the Constitution; reference to *Afjal Ansari v. State of U.P.* (2023).
note.Exam angle: Criminal Procedure Code – application of Section 389(1) in the context of electoral politics; could be asked as an issue-framing question on the limits of seeking stay of conviction under the Representation of the People Act or on the interplay between Article 21 and criminal convictions.

title: Whether Magistrate's Order Directing FIR Registration Is Revisable? J&K High Court Refers Legal Question To Larger Bench
court: Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh High Court
summary: The Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh High Court has referred to a larger Bench the question whether an order passed by a Magistrate under Section 156(3) CrPC, directing registration of an FIR and police investigation, is an interlocutory order barred from revision or an intermediate order amenable to revisional jurisdiction.

note.Facts: Two petitions challenged orders of Judicial Magistrates directing registration of FIRs under Section 156(3) CrPC; the petitioners argued that such orders are interlocutory and not subject to criminal revision, while the respondents contended they are intermediate orders amenable to revision.
note.Issue: Whether an order passed by a Magistrate under Section 156(3) CrPC directing FIR registration and investigation is an interlocutory order barred by Sections 397(2) CrPC and 438(2) BNSS, or an intermediate order subject to criminal revision.
note.Held: The Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh High Court did not decide the issue but referred six specific questions to a larger Bench for authoritative determination.
note.Principle: The nature of an order (interlocutory vs. intermediate) must be examined by its jurisdiction, issue decided, effect and legal consequences; mere non-determination of guilt does not automatically render it interlocutory, and an order may acquire revisional jurisdiction if it decides a substantial legal right or jurisdictional question.
note.Provisions: State of Haryana*, *Madhu Limaye v. State of Maharashtra*, *Girish Kumar Suneja v. CBI*, *Father Thomas v. State of U.P.* (Allahabad HC), *Arun P. Gidh v. Chandraprakash Singh* (Bombay HC), *Manohar Nath Sher v. State of J&K*, *Satpal Sharma v. Pawan Singh Rathore*, *Anurag Bhatnagar & Anr. v. State (NCT of Delhi)*, *Priyanka Srivastava v. State of Uttar Pradesh*, *Anil Kumar v. M.K. Aiyappa*.
note.Exam angle: Criminal Procedure Code – test the revisional jurisdiction under Section 397 CrPC vis-à-vis orders under Section 156(3) CrPC; focus on distinguishing interlocutory and intermediate orders and the impact of Supreme Court precedents (Amar Nath, Madhu Limaye, Suneja).

title: Supreme Court Dismisses PIL Seeking Ban On Animal Sacrifices For Religious Rituals
summary: The Supreme Court today dismissed a public interest litigation seeking a ban on killing of animals in the name of religion. A bench of Justice Vikram Nath, Justice R Mahadevan, and Justice Aparesh.

note.Facts: A public interest litigation was filed by Advocate Shruti Bist seeking a direction to the Ministry of Animal Husbandry to amend Section 28 of the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, to prohibit killing animals in the name of religion.
note.Issue: Whether the saving clause in Section 28, which exempts animal killing required by any religion, can be struck down or amended to ban animal sacrifice.
note.Held: The Supreme Court, a bench of Justices Vikram Nath, R Mahadevan and Aparesh Singh, dismissed the PIL and did not order any amendment to Section 28.
note.Principle: A statutory saving clause that expressly protects religiously mandated animal killing cannot be overridden by a PIL; the Court will not interfere with a clear legislative provision on religious practice.
note.Provisions: Section 28 of the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960; no other statutes, articles or cases are cited in the source.
note.Exam angle: Questions may test the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, focusing on the interpretation of Section 28’s savings clause and its interaction with constitutional guarantees of religious freedom.

summary: The Telangana High Court has recently quashed the detention orders of six individuals over the murder of Communist Party of India leader Kethawat Chandu Rathod, consequently classified as 'Goondas' under the Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities Act, 1986. The Division Bench comprising of Justice Moushumi Bhattacharya and Justice Renuka Yara said that a single crime.

note.Facts: Six persons were detained as “Goondas” under the Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities Act, 1986 for the murder of CPI leader Kethawat Chandu Rathod.
note.Issue: Whether a single criminal act (the murder) suffices to classify the accused as habitual offenders (“Goondas”) under the Act.
note.Held: The Telangana High Court quashed the preventive detention orders, holding that a single crime does not meet the statutory requirement of habitual offending.
note.Principle: Classification as a “Goonda” under the Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities Act, 1986 requires proof of a pattern of repeated offences; a solitary offence is insufficient.
note.Provisions: Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities Act, 1986 (specific sections not stated in the source).

title: Hindu Marriage Can't Be Dissolved Through Community Separation Deed Unless Custom Is Established: Rajasthan High Court
ratio: A Hindu marriage cannot be treated as dissolved merely on the basis of a community separation deed unless the customary practice permitting such dissolution is…
summary: The ruling: A Hindu marriage cannot be treated as dissolved merely on the basis of a community separation deed unless the customary practice permitting such dissolution is….

note.Facts: The appellant sought recognition of a marriage dissolution based solely on a community separation deed, which the Family Court had refused to acknowledge.
note.Issue: Whether a Hindu marriage can be deemed dissolved merely on the basis of a community separation deed absent proof of a customary practice allowing such dissolution.
note.Held: The Rajasthan High Court dismissed the appeal, holding that a Hindu marriage cannot be dissolved through a community separation deed unless the existence of a custom permitting such dissolution is duly established.
note.Principle: A Hindu marriage is not dissolved by a community separation deed unless the custom that authorises such dissolution is proven.
note.Exam angle: Hindu Marriage Act – test of custom as a ground for dissolution; could be asked to frame the issue of “custom” as an ingredient for nullity or dissolution of marriage.

title: “Legislature cannot nullify a judgment by enacting law without removing the basis”: Andhra Pradesh High Court strikes down Section 147-A, Income-tax Act, 1961 as unconstitutional
summary: Andhra Pradesh High Court: The petitions were filed challenging the constitutional validity of Section 147-A, Income-tax Act, 1961 (IT Act), inserted by the Finance Act, 2026 , with retrospective effect from 1 April 2021, as being ultra vires and violative of the basic structure of the Constitution , including the principles of Rule of Law.

note.Facts: Petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of the newly inserted Section 147-A of the Income-Tax Act, 1961 (effective 1 April 2026 but retrospectively deemed from 1 April 2021), alleging it was ultra-vires and violated the basic structure, Rule of Law and separation of powers, and also contested reassessment proceedings initiated by Jurisdictional Assessing Officers (JAOs) under Sections 148-A and 148 as being non-faceless and therefore without jurisdiction.
note.Issue: Whether a legislature can nullify a judicial pronouncement by enacting a retrospective provision (Section 147-A) without removing the basis of the earlier judgment, and whether the JAOs have jurisdiction to issue notices and conduct reassessment under the faceless assessment scheme.
note.Held: The Andhra Pradesh High Court struck down Section 147-A as unconstitutional and set aside the impugned reassessment proceedings, holding that the provision sought to override judicial findings without eliminating the defect identified by the courts and could not be inserted after the IT Act had been repealed.
note.Principle: A validating or retrospective enactment cannot stand if it does not remove the defect identified by the judiciary; the legislature cannot defeat a judgment by merely inserting a new provision without addressing the underlying basis of the decision.
note.Provisions: Sections 147-A, 148-A, 148, 151-A, 144-B of the Income-Tax Act, 1961; Finance Acts 2021, 2022, 2026; Notification No. 18/2022, 15/2022, 61/2022; cases Snehdham Trust v. CIT (2025) SCC OnLine Guj 5771, Prithvi Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Broach Borough Municipality (1969) 2 SCC 283.
note.Exam angle: Income-Tax Act – validity of retrospective/validating legislation under the Constitution (basic structure, Rule of Law). Could be asked as: *“Explain the limitation on Parliament’s power to enact retrospective provisions that seek to override judicial decisions, citing the Andhra Pradesh High Court’s decision on Section 147-A.”

title: Offering money, catching hold of a woman’s hand and asking her to accompany him to the jungle outrages her modesty: Himachal Pradesh High Court
summary: Himachal Pradesh HC : The present criminal revision petition, challenging a decision by the Additional Session Judge, dealt with a conviction of an accused under Section 354 , Penal Code, 1860 (IPC) arising from an incident where he allegedly caught hold of the informant’s arm, offered her money, and asked her to accompany him to.

note.Facts: The informant was returning from the jungle when the accused offered her ₹100, caught hold of her arm/hand and asked her to accompany him to the jungle; she raised an alarm, witnesses arrived, and the accused fled.
note.Issue: Whether the accused’s conduct of offering money, seizing the woman’s hand and urging her to follow him amounts to “outraging the modesty” of a woman punishable under Section 354 IPC.
note.Held: The High Court dismissed the revision, affirming the conviction and sentence under Section 354 IPC, holding that the accused’s acts indeed outraged the informant’s modesty.
note.Principle: Any act that shocks the sense of decency of a woman and assaults her modesty, such as offering money and forcibly taking hold of her hand to lead her elsewhere, falls within Section 354 IPC; a hostile witness’s testimony is not to be discarded if corroborated by other evidence.
note.Provisions: Section 354, Indian Penal Code; Section 313, Criminal Procedure Code; cited cases – *Kuntegowda v. Thurubaiah* (2026 SCC OnLine SC 1485), *State of Maharashtra v. Jagmohan Singh Kuldip Singh Anand* (2004 7 SCC 659), *State of Kerala v. Puttumana Illath Jathavedan Namboodiri* (1999 2 SCC 452), *Dadu v. State of M.P.* (2025 SCC OnLine SC 2733), *Selvamani v. State of T.N.* (2024 SCC OnLine SC 837), *Krishnan v. State of T.N.* (2003 7 SCC 56), *Rupan Deol Bajaj v. Kanwar Pal Singh Gill* (1995 6 SCC 194), *Tarkeshwar Sahu v. State of Bihar* (2006 8 SCC 560), *State of Punjab v. Major Singh* (1966 SCC OnLine SC 51).
note.Exam angle: IPC 354 – elements of outraging a woman’s modesty; evidentiary rule on hostile witnesses (corroboration required). Could be asked as: “Explain the test for ‘outraging modesty’ under Section 354 IPC and discuss the treatment of hostile witness testimony.”
